Adopted in 2019, the EU Directive on single-use plastics targets the ten single-use plastic items most often found on European beaches, together with fishing gear. The measures differ according to whether sustainable alternatives exist. Where alternatives are readily available and affordable, products such as plastic cutlery, plates, straws, cotton bud sticks and expanded polystyrene food containers were banned from the EU market from July 2021.

For products without such alternatives, including tobacco filters and wet wipes, the Directive relies on other tools. Member States must reduce the consumption of plastic food containers and drinks cups, and producers of the products concerned must contribute to the costs of waste management and of cleaning up litter under 'extended producer responsibility' schemes. Certain products must also carry a label informing consumers about the plastic they contain and the appropriate way to dispose of them.

Covered plastic beverage bottles of up to three litres are subject to specific targets: they must contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025 for PET bottles and 30% by 2030 for all such bottles, and Member States must collect 77% of them separately by 2025 and 90% by 2029. Since July 2024, caps and lids have had to remain attached during use on covered beverage containers of up to three litres.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: All plastic drinks bottles had to contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025.
Wherever an alternative to a plastic product exists, the plastic version has been banned, whatever the price.
Producers of tobacco filters have to help pay for cleaning up the litter their products cause.
Tethered caps have largely solved the problem of bottle lids on European beaches.

REACH, the EU regulation on chemicals that entered into force in 2007, places the burden of proof on industry rather than on public authorities. Companies that manufacture or import a chemical substance in quantities of one tonne or more per year must register it with the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) in Helsinki, providing information on its properties, its uses and how it can be handled safely; standard information requirements increase at tonnage-band boundaries, including ten tonnes, rather than at every increase in quantity. This registration duty does not apply below the one-tonne threshold. The principle is often summarised as 'no data, no market': a substance that has not been registered cannot be manufactured or placed on the EU market in those quantities.

Substances of very high concern, such as those that cause cancer or accumulate in living organisms, can be placed on a list from which they may be moved to an authorisation list. Once that happens, they can be used only with a specific authorisation, which is granted only if the risks are adequately controlled or if the socio-economic benefits outweigh them and no suitable alternative exists. Certain uses of other substances can also be restricted across the EU.

Environmental organisations argue that identifying and restricting harmful chemicals takes too long, while industry points to the high cost of registration for small companies.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Companies must register every substance they make or import under REACH, whatever the quantity.
A firm producing ten tonnes of a substance a year must supply more data than one producing two.
The cost of registration is likely to have driven a number of small firms out of the EU market.
Any substance found to cause cancer is automatically placed on the authorisation list.

When consumers buy goods online or by phone from a trader in the EU, they generally have 14 days to cancel the purchase without giving any reason. For goods, the period usually starts on the day the goods are delivered, and it remains available for twelve months after the original period ends if the trader never informs the consumer of this right. After cancelling, the consumer must return the goods, and the trader must refund all payments received, including standard delivery costs, within 14 days of being informed of withdrawal. Unless it offers collection, the trader may withhold reimbursement until it receives the goods or evidence of their return. The consumer may have to pay the cost of sending the goods back if the trader made this clear beforehand.

Some products are excluded from this right of withdrawal, such as goods made to the consumer's specifications, perishable items like fresh food, and sealed hygiene products that have been unsealed after delivery. Digital content such as a downloaded film can also be excluded once the download has started, with prior express consent and acknowledgement of losing the withdrawal right.

Separately from the right of withdrawal, sellers must provide a legal guarantee of at least two years, under which they must repair, replace or refund goods that turn out to be faulty. For defects that appear within the first year, it is generally presumed that they already existed at the time of delivery.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Most consumers who cancel online purchases do so within the first week.
Any defect that shows up during the two-year guarantee is presumed to have existed at delivery.
Every product bought online can be returned within 14 days without giving a reason.
For a purchase otherwise eligible for withdrawal, a shopper never told of the right to cancel still has it ten months after delivery.

The Pact on Migration and Asylum, a package of ten legislative acts formally adopted in May 2024, was designed to apply as a whole from 2026. One of its most debated elements is a new solidarity mechanism, intended to share responsibility between Member States more evenly than the previous rules did.

The mechanism is often described as mandatory but flexible. Each year, the Commission assesses which Member States are under migratory pressure and proposes the size of an annual solidarity pool, which the Council then establishes. Reference planning uses at least 30,000 relocations and EUR 600 million annually, with financial contributions valued at EUR 20,000 per relocation-equivalent. These are collective planning references, not a duty for every state to both relocate and pay. Member States must contribute their fair share, although those under migratory pressure can ask for a reduction, and each chooses how to contribute: by relocating applicants from countries under pressure, by making financial contributions, or by funding operational and capacity-building measures. No Member State can be obliged to carry out relocations.

Supporters argue that this flexibility made agreement possible after years of deadlock over earlier reform proposals. Critics on one side say that allowing states to pay instead of relocating weakens the principle of shared responsibility; critics on the other side object to any compulsory element at all. How the mechanism works in practice will depend largely on the pledges that Member States make.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The Commission can require a Member State to relocate applicants if that state has pledged too little to the annual pool.
Critics of the mechanism agree that letting states pay rather than relocate weakens the principle of shared responsibility.
The financial contributions are paid into the EU budget and are mainly used to fund surveillance of the external borders.
Choosing not to relocate anyone does not by itself free a Member State from contributing to the pool.

Every citizen of the Union has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States, but under the 2004 Citizens' Rights Directive that right is graded according to the length of stay. For up to three months, a citizen needs nothing more than a valid identity card or passport. Beyond three months, the right of residence depends on the person's situation: workers and self-employed people qualify, while students and economically inactive people must have sufficient resources not to become a burden on the host state's social assistance system, as well as comprehensive sickness insurance. Host states may require registration with the authorities after three months.

After five years of continuous legal residence, a citizen acquires the right of permanent residence, which is no longer subject to these conditions. It is lost only through absence from the host state for more than two consecutive years. Family members, including those who are not themselves EU citizens, enjoy rights derived from the citizen's.

Protection against expulsion also increases over time. A host state may restrict free movement on grounds of public policy, public security or public health, and restrictions must be proportionate. Public-policy and public-security measures must be based exclusively on personal conduct; public-health measures follow separate rules. Once a citizen has resided in the host state for the previous ten years, expulsion is possible only on imperative grounds of public security.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Students moving to another Member State must usually prove a minimum monthly income that is set at EU level.
Every host state requires citizens from other Member States to register with the authorities after three months.
Family members who are not EU citizens acquire a right of permanent residence only after ten years.
An economically inactive citizen with six years of continuous legal residence in a host state no longer has to prove sufficient resources.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is designed to put a fair price on the carbon emitted during the production of certain goods entering the EU. It addresses 'carbon leakage': the risk that production moves to countries with weaker climate policies, or that EU products are replaced by more carbon-intensive imports, which would shift emissions abroad rather than reduce them. The mechanism covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.

During a transitional phase from October 2023 to the end of 2025, importers only had to report the emissions embedded in their goods; no payment was due. The definitive regime began in January 2026. Importers must now be authorised and will surrender CBAM certificates whose price follows that of allowances in the EU Emissions Trading System. If a carbon price has already been paid in the country of production, it can be deducted from the amount owed. A 2025 simplification introduced an annual net-mass exemption of no more than 50 tonnes for relevant covered goods; electricity and hydrogen are excluded from that exemption. It removed most importers while retaining the vast majority of embedded emissions.

At the same time, the free emission allowances that EU producers in the same sectors have received are being phased out gradually between 2026 and 2034, so that domestic and imported goods face a comparable carbon cost.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The mechanism ensures that imported and EU-made goods always bear exactly the same carbon cost, whatever the sector.
Since the 2025 simplification, the mechanism no longer applies to most of the emissions embedded in imports of covered goods.
Revenue from the sale of CBAM certificates is to be paid mainly into the EU budget rather than kept by the Member States.
A cement importer can deduct a carbon price already paid where the cement was made from what it owes under CBAM.

The Pay Transparency Directive, adopted in 2023, aims to enforce the principle of equal pay for men and women for equal work or work of equal value. Member States had until June 2026 to bring it into national law. Several of its rights apply to all employers, whatever their size. Job applicants must be told the starting pay, or its range, early enough for informed, transparent pay negotiation, for example through the vacancy notice or before the interview, and employers may no longer ask candidates how much they earned in previous jobs. Workers may request information on their own pay level and on average pay levels, broken down by sex, for colleagues doing the same work or work of equal value. Contract terms that prevent workers from disclosing their pay in order to enforce equal pay are not allowed.

Reporting duties, by contrast, depend on size. Employers with at least 250 workers must report on their gender pay gap every year, those with 150 to 249 workers every three years, and those with 100 to 149 workers also every three years but only from a later date. Smaller employers have no such duty under the Directive, though Member States may impose one. Where reporting reveals a gap of at least 5% in any category of workers that the employer cannot justify on objective, gender-neutral grounds and does not correct within six months, a joint pay assessment must be carried out with workers' representatives.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Employers with 100 or more workers must report annually on the gender pay gap within their organisation.
Employers who ask job candidates about their previous salaries will face fines that are set at EU level.
A joint pay assessment is required wherever the overall gap between men's and women's pay exceeds 5%.
A company with 30 employees still owes candidates early starting-pay information, despite having no reporting duty under the Directive.

A fictional packaging standard recognises three certification classes. All class P products have passed a pressure test. The test-based waiver route requires both pressure testing and an independent seal check. Class Q registration, by contrast, concerns the maker's reporting system and says nothing about either test. Products can hold more than one class at once.

No product containing liquid can use the ordinary paperwork-only waiver route. Other products can obtain such a waiver without pressure testing if their paperwork is complete. The register records that a product has a waiver, but does not identify the route used. It records certification classes separately, and the absence of a class Q entry is not evidence that testing failed. The authority registered 90 products in the latest quarter, with overlapping categories.

Product Pine contains liquid and has an ordinary transport waiver valid for its present shipment. The authority confirms that the waiver was granted through one of the stated routes, with no special dispensation. Pine's class P and Q fields have not been published. Product Cedar is known to hold class P and class Q, but no seal-check finding or waiver decision for Cedar has been released. Both products have completed the maker's internal inspection, a procedure separate from the independent seal check.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Cedar's two published classes establish the independent seal check, so its waiver status can be inferred without a separate decision.
Pine's waiver entails both tests; Cedar's two classes establish pressure testing and reporting, but do not establish its waiver.
Every waived product is pressure-tested, since the paperwork-only route is unavailable for the liquid carried in Pine's shipment.
Pine cannot hold class Q because its waiver depended on testing rather than the maker's reporting system.

A fictional park programme offers evening access to residents with either a local keycard or a permit from a participating school. Every local keycard holder has completed an identity check. A school permit can be issued without that check, but everyone entering on a school permit must enter with a named supervisor from the programme's roster present, including adult permit-holders. Holding both documents is permitted.

Adults can enter without a supervisor when using a local keycard. Children require a rostered supervisor regardless of entry document. A supervisor's presence does not by itself confer an entry document. The gate log lists lawful evening admissions and ages but does not identify the document used. It does not record identity checks or distinguish group visits from solo visits.

The log includes an adult, Orla, lawfully admitted without any rostered supervisor present, and a child, Ren, lawfully admitted with a supervisor. Orla's and Ren's document files are not released. The programme confirms that no admission used an exception or a document other than the two stated kinds. Their names are not sufficient to identify relationships to the participating schools. The report gives no evidence about whether Ren held one entry document or both, or whether Ren had independently completed an identity check.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every lawful admission establishes a completed identity check, because a local keycard is one of the two permitted evening-entry documents.
Orla's entry entails a keycard and identity check; Ren's supervisor does not distinguish the two permissible entry routes.
Children entering on a local keycard need no rostered supervisor, so Ren's accompanying supervisor establishes use of a school permit.
Orla was unrelated to the participating schools because an adult without a supervisor could not have any connection to their permit arrangements.

A fictional school serves unchanged standard meals under a standing approval. A meal is changed when its ingredient source changes or when preparation introduces a new cross-contact route. Using an identical recipe name does not make it unchanged. A changed meal requires either an approved supplier declaration or an on-site allergen review. A supplier declaration covers only the factory and ingredient lot named on it.

An on-site review uses a trained allergen lead, with either direct kitchen observation or continuous live video. Both require the lead to verify the actual preparation line after the change. Training ceases to be current after a new national allergen protocol unless a protocol supplement is passed. The supplement can be assessed by an external trainer or a school consortium; either assessor must be independent of the lead's meal-preparation work. The lead's kitchen supervisor cannot independently assess it. Menu pages publish meal names rather than training and review records.

The allergen review took place after the new protocol came into effect. A meal was validly served after both its ingredient source and lot changed to ones outside the supplier declaration. The sole allergen lead's training predated the new protocol. The recipe name was unchanged, and the kitchen supervisor offered an endorsement. No other declaration, lead or approval route existed.
stem: Which of the following statements is supported by the passage?
options: The unchanged recipe name preserved standing approval despite the ingredient-lot change, so no independent protocol supplement or on-site allergen review was needed.
The kitchen supervisor’s endorsement supplied the independent supplement assessment because that supervisor already understood the lead’s meal-preparation work.
The lead verified the preparation line by continuous live video rather than direct observation because the protocol supplement was assessed by a consortium.
The allergen lead had passed a protocol supplement assessed independently of the preparation work and verified the actual changed preparation line.
